cards.text: This is a song of ascents from Solomon, king of Israel (1 Kings 2:12). He sings about a house going up and a city with watchmen standing guard. And he's got one big condition hanging over both of them.

cards.question: Builders can labor on a house all they want. Solomon says their labor is in vain unless what?

cards.text: Now the city. The watchmen stand guard with their eyes wide open, and I know that look, friend, because I wore it in the back of a junk drawer for YEARS.

cards.question: True or false: Solomon says the city is safe as long as the watchmen stand guard.

cards.text: Then Solomon turns to the worker who rises early and stays up late, toiling for bread to eat. That's a baker's schedule, and my oven timer is TIRED of me.

cards.question: Solomon says all that early rising and late toiling is in vain, for He gives ___ to His beloved.

cards.text: He gives SLEEP to His beloved, and friend, I have never felt so seen by a verse in my life. Then Solomon turns from houses and cities to children.

cards.question: Solomon calls children a heritage. Where does he say that heritage comes from?
True or false: Solomon calls the fruit of the womb the LORD's reward.
Solomon paints a picture of children born in one's youth. He says they're like what in the hand of a warrior?

cards.text: If children are arrows, then "Blessed is the man whose quiver is full of them." Six cookie cutters, friend, my quiver was FULL, and Mags made sure the whole kitchen heard about it.

cards.question: Solomon says the man with a full quiver will not be put to shame. When?

answers.text: When he confronts enemies at the gate
When he stands before the king
When he brings his offering to the priest

cards.text: Next up is another song of ascents, and this one has no name on it. It's a mystery, friend, like a cookie box left on the counter with no tag, and you KNOW I'm still opening it. And it opens with a blessing.

cards.question: This song opens by calling someone blessed. Who?

answers.text: All who rise early to work

cards.text: Remember all that toiling in vain back in Psalm 127? This song talks about your labor too, but now you get to EAT its fruit, and friend, I'm a stamper who has pressed ten thousand cookies and never tasted ONE.

cards.question: When you eat the fruit of your labor, what does this song say will be yours?

cards.text: Then the song walks right into the house and looks around the table, like a guest who showed up early and is now checking out EVERYTHING.

cards.question: In this song, the wife is like something flourishing within the house. What is it?
True or false: The song pictures the sons like young cedars sitting around the table.

cards.text: Sons like olive shoots sitting around the table, and olive shoots just SIT there, friend. My Chip sat around the mixing bowl too, and it was "Papa, one more story" EVERY. SINGLE. NIGHT.

cards.question: The song sums it up: In this way indeed shall ___ come to the man who fears the LORD.

cards.text: Then the song says, "May the LORD bless you from Zion," and friend, after years of listening to the dead batteries I shared a drawer with argue all night, THAT is a sentence I would frame.

cards.question: True or false: The song says may the LORD bless you from Zion so that you may see the prosperity of Jerusalem all the days of your life.
There's one more thing the song says you may see. What is it?

cards.text: The song hopes you'll see GRANDKIDS, and I think a stamper's grandkids would come out as crumbs, and I would LOVE every crumb. Then it closes with one last line for the whole nation: "Peace be upon Israel!"

findings.problem: Psalm 127:2 speaks to 'you' ('In vain you rise early and stay up late'). The card says Solomon 'turns to the worker,' which names an addressee the text doesn't name.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: No story card sets up the warrior picture. The baker must pick between arrows, swords and shields, all of which fit 'in the hand of a warrior.' Getting it right is luck, like the Psalm 23 oil example.

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

findings.problem: This story card has 3 sentences. It isn't the walkthrough's opening card, so it should have 1 or 2.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: Psalm 128:1 defines those who fear the LORD as those 'who walk in His ways.' No card tells or asks about this, so the baker misses a key detail of the psalm's opening blessing.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: The card sets Psalm 127's 'toiling in vain' against Psalm 128 ('but now you get to EAT its fruit'). Neither text states that contrast. Psalm 128:2 also says 'when you eat,' and the card turns that into a promise.

rule.text: Connecting passages. When he connects two passages, or explains what a law was for, he says only what the texts state.

findings.problem: Card 5 gives no hint toward the vine picture, so the baker is guessing between a vine, a cedar and a palm. Getting it right is luck.

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

findings.problem: Nothing before this card lets the baker reason whether the sons are like cedars or something else. It's a coin-flip guess about a detail of the picture.

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.

findings.problem: The card says Chip 'sat around the mixing bowl' asking for stories every night. In the backstory, Chip asked for stories 'every night after the kitchen went dark.' The mixing-bowl scene adds something new to the backstory.

rule.text: His own world isn't Bible fact. His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them.

findings.problem: The true or false statement just restates Psalm 128:5, including the 'prosperity of Jerusalem' clause the baker hasn't seen. It tests wording, not meaning, and the baker can only guess.

rule.text: Ask about the movement and the meaning: what changes, what the picture is, why the speaker says what he says.

findings.problem: The joke that a stamper's grandkids 'would come out as crumbs' doesn't click. His kids are cookie cutters, and it's unclear why their kids would be crumbs.

rule.text: If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it.
